title: Chapter 65 — The Whale as a Dish
paragraphs: That mortal man should feed upon the creature that feeds his lamp, and, like Stubb, eat him by his own light, as you might say — this seems so outlandish a thing that one must go a little into the history and philosophy of it.

It is on record that three centuries ago, the tongue of the Right Whale was considered a great delicacy in France and commanded high prices there. Also, that in Henry VIII's time, a certain cook of the court obtained a handsome reward for inventing an admirable sauce to be eaten with barbecued porpoises, which, you remember, are a species of whale. Porpoises, indeed, are to this day considered fine eating. The meat is made into balls about the size of billiard balls, and being well seasoned and spiced, might be taken for turtle-balls or veal-balls.

The fact is that among his hunters at least, the whale would be considered a noble dish by all hands, were there not so much of him. But when you come to sit down before a meat-pie nearly one hundred feet long, it takes away your appetite. Only the most unprejudiced of men like Stubb nowadays eat cooked whale. But the Eskimos are not so fastidious. Among the Eskimos of Greenland, whale steak is a common dish.

But what further degrades the whale as a civilized dish is his excessive richness. He is the great prize ox of the sea, too fat to be delicately good. Look at his hump, which would be as fine eating as the buffalo's — which is esteemed a rare treat — were it not such a solid pyramid of fat. But the spermaceti itself, how bland and creamy that is. Like the butter in rich pastries.

In the case of a small Sperm Whale, the brains are considered a fine dish. The case of the skull is cracked open with an axe, and the two plump, whitish lobes are withdrawn — they look precisely like two large puddings. They are then mixed with flour and cooked into a most delicious dish, something like calves' head in flavor, which is quite a dish among some epicures.

It is not perhaps entirely because the whale is so excessively greasy that landsmen seem to regard eating him with disgust. That seems to come, in some way, from the consideration previously mentioned: that a man should eat a freshly killed creature of the sea, and eat it by its own light. But no doubt the first man who ever murdered an ox was regarded with the same horror. And yet that same first ox was eaten with great relish. Go to the meat-market of a Saturday night and see the crowds of live bipeds staring up at the long rows of dead quadrupeds. Does not that sight take a tooth out of the cannibal's criticism?

But Stubb — he eats the whale by its own light, does he? And that is adding insult to injury, is it? Look at your knife-handle there, my civilized and enlightened gourmet, dining on that roast beef — what is that handle made of? Nothing but the bones of the brother of the very ox you are eating! And what do you pick your teeth with after devouring that fat goose? With a feather of the same bird. And with what quill did the Secretary of the Society for the Suppression of Cruelty to Animals formally write his protest against the use of whalebone corsets? With a quill from a goose.
